note: Proposed, not sealed. Dogfooding feedback on nestor ui: 'the Signals view is just three cards, and nothing has shown up for me in a month'. The three cards are alarms (overruled seals, repeatedly-refused queries, junk pairs) that rarely fire for a low-volume solo store, so the tab read as broken. The operator's steer was broader: 'this should also be a place we can show behavior in other directions — Nestor can show a LOT of things, and a lot of it isn't viable in the UI.' A grounded survey of what the package computes but never surfaces confirmed three cheap, high-value signals already produced and read by nothing in the UI. Front-end plus one small read-only endpoint; the operator chose the three surfaced here (unevidenced seals and threshold calibration were offered and deferred). Pinned in tests/test_ui.py and tests/test_misses.py.

decisions.question: The Signals tab is three failure-alarm cards that are empty for a healthy solo store, so it reads as useless. Reframe the emptiness, or make the tab carry more of what Nestor knows?
decisions.commitment: Both, as a health panel. Alarms (overruled seals, junk pairs, and newly sealed-but-unverifiable rows) come first under an 'Alarms' heading with a header badge that reads 'all clear' when they are all empty — empty is the good state and now says so. Below them, a 'Coverage & upkeep' group carries signals that are informative even on a healthy store: seals due for re-verification, coverage misses, and the existing repeatedly-refused-queries card (the calibration hint). The replaced-seals card always renders because it carries the 'include self-corrections' toggle.
decisions.why: The operator's own read — three blank cards look broken, not clear — is the finding: alarms need a resting state that says 'nothing is wrong', and the tab needs content that exists on a quiet store. 'A survey is good for finding, not asserting' (decision 1878ea86): the three added signals were found by survey and each confirmed against the tree before wiring — /api/due-for-reverification exists (nestor/ui.py) and its own docstring says it is 'an API endpoint the Signals tab can consume', yet ui_page.py called it nowhere; the sealed-unverifiable list is already served by /api/pairs?unverifiable=1; coverage misses are recorded on every unanswered ask and read by nothing. All three are read-only and cheap (the misses read is indexed SQL, no scan).

decisions.question: Coverage misses (nestor.misses) are computed on every ask but have no API route and no CLI command. How does the UI read them, and does it leak the queries?
decisions.commitment: A new read-only GET /api/misses returns nestor.misses.coverage verbatim — {supported, distinct_misses, total_misses, surfaced, withheld, queue} — and the Signals card renders the queue (queries missed more than once, with their text and sighting count) and states the withheld count. It never shows the text of a one-off. The endpoint reads the miss ledger only; there is no POST counterpart.
decisions.why: misses.coverage already enforces the privacy gate — a query seen once is counted in `withheld` but its text is not returned (misses.py: only rows past the k>=2 gate carry text) — so the endpoint that surfaces it inherits that, and the card states the withheld size rather than hiding that it is hiding something. A miss is never a proposal and is never served (the query_misses table is documented as never-served), so exposing it read-only in Signals cannot change what Nestor answers. The endpoint returns {supported:false} rather than erroring on a store without the misses capability, matching how the tab's other cards degrade.
